papers.title: Modified Long-Acting UCN2 Promotes Fat Mass Loss While Preserving Skeletal Muscle Mass and Function in Mouse Models of Pharmacological Weight Loss and Sarcopenic Obesity
papers.abstract: No approved pharmacotherapy simultaneously reduces excess adiposity and preserves skeletal muscle mass and function. Such an agent would have two distinct applications: improvement of the quality of pharmacological weight loss and treatment of sarcopenic obesity. Urocortin 2 (UCN2) and its receptor corticotropin-releasing hormone receptor 2 (CRHR2) are highly expressed in skeletal muscle, where they regulate hypertrophy and metabolism. Here we show that a modified long-acting acylated UCN2 peptide reduces fat mass while preserving muscle mass and enhancing function across distinct mouse models. Pair-feeding showed these effects were independent of reduced food intake. Combined with the GLP-1 receptor agonist semaglutide or the GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist retatrutide, UCN2 produced the greatest magnitude of fat loss while preserving lean and muscle mass and increasing in vivo force production, and this gain persisted 4 weeks after dosing stopped. UCN2 increased energy expenditure, prevented the adaptive fall in expenditure caused by reduced food intake, and promoted whole-body fatty acid oxidation. In a sarcopenic obese mouse model, UCN2 reduced fat mass while increasing muscle mass, muscle function, and myofibrillar protein synthesis. These findings identify UCN2-CRHR2 signaling as a strategy to uncouple fat loss from muscle loss, both as a standalone therapy for sarcopenic obesity and as a combination partner with incretins.

papers.title: RETRO-URETERAL DELIVERY OF AAV-KP VECTORS FOR RENAL GENE TRANSFER AND THE ASSESSMENT OF TRANSGENE REABSORPTION IN THE KIDNEY
papers.abstract: Monogenic disorders cause a substantial fraction of chronic kidney disease, yet no renal gene therapy exists, partly because adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors transduce the kidney poorly after systemic delivery. Screening a barcoded library of 80 natural and chimeric AAV serotypes administered retrogradely into the mouse renal pelvis identified AAV-KP1, AAV-KP2 and AAV-KP3 as enriched in the injected kidney but not in the liver. Individual validation confirmed efficient transduction of the administered kidney, with vector genome copy numbers approaching hepatic levels, 50- to 500-fold above the contralateral kidney and far above AAV9. Using kidney-specific (KSPC) and ubiquitous (CMV) promoters, transduction was detected in collecting duct, distal convoluted tubule, proximal tubule, Bowman's capsule, interstitial cells and podocytes, with cell-type coverage depending on the promoter. Unexpectedly, GFP and mCherry protein was abundant in proximal tubules of kidneys lacking transgene mRNA, including contralateral and intravenously dosed kidneys. RNA-FISH, vector genome quantification and serum mCherry indicate that this protein derives from circulating transgene product filtered and reabsorbed by the proximal tubule rather than from local transduction. Retrograde delivery of AAV-KP capsids therefore achieves broad renal epithelial transduction, and transgene mRNA must be assessed alongside protein if kidney-tropic capsids are to be ranked reliably.

papers.title: Energetic costs of osmo- and ionoregulatory responses to desiccation and recovery in a model insect
papers.abstract: Climate change is expected to increase the frequency, duration and intensity of weather events that cause desiccation stress to small-bodied terrestrial insects. Whether a desiccation event may cause mortality depends on the time-dependent osmo- and ionoregulation responses of insects to desiccation and their recovery. Yet these responses and their associated energetic costs are not always clear for a range of mesic species. Here, we characterised the ability of house crickets (Acheta domesticus) to physiologically resist and recover from desiccation. We measured water loss from different tissues, changes in haemolymph volume and in haemolymph ion concentration as well as stored macromolecules (lipids, carbohydrates and proteins) use over a time-course of desiccation (0, 3, 6 or 18 h) and recovery with access to water and with or without access to food (18 h desiccation and 6 h recovery). During 18 h of desiccation, crickets regulated haemolymph ion concentration, avoiding hyperkalaemia and hypernatraemia, despite losing up to 14.5 and 21.1% of their body water for female and males respectively, across all body compartments. Recovery represented a distinct physiological phase to acute stress with a restoration of ion concentrations and body water with significant energetic contributions from stored macromolecules. We conclude crickets employ a general two-phase physiological strategy to withstand and recover from a short-term acute desiccation stress, establishing a physiological baseline to evaluate potential desiccation stress, and providing key insight into the time-dependency of osmoregulation and ion regulation for insects encountering fluctuating desiccation stress under climate change.

papers.title: Myeloid mDIC Deficiency Remodels Adipose Macrophages to an Efferocytosis-Associated State and Improves Metabolic Homeostasis During Obesity
papers.abstract: Obesity-associated adipose inflammation contributes to metabolic dysfunction, yet the mechanisms linking mitochondrial metabolism to macrophage efferocytosis remain incompletely understood. The mitochondrial dicarboxylate carrier (mDIC), encoded by SLC25A10, regulates adipocyte function, but its role in macrophages remains unclear. Here, we investigated how myeloid mDIC deficiency affects mitochondrial function, macrophage heterogeneity, and metabolic homeostasis during diet-induced obesity. We observed reduced mDIC protein expression in subcutaneous white adipose tissue from individuals with obesity, whereas palmitate increased mDIC expression in mouse and human macrophages. Myeloid mDIC deletion preserved mitochondrial respiration under palmitate stress. Single-cell RNA sequencing of adipose stromal vascular cells from high-fat diet (HFD)-fed mice revealed an expanded efferocytosis-associated macrophage population and reduced proportions of inflammatory and lipid-associated macrophages. Consistently, mDIC-deficient macrophages exhibited increased Mertk expression and greater association with apoptotic cells. Pharmacological inhibition of mitochondrial ATP synthase or electron transport markedly suppressed apoptotic cell uptake, including the quenching-resistant fraction, without substantially affecting macrophage viability. In vivo, myeloid mDIC deletion attenuated HFD-induced weight gain, improved insulin sensitivity, and increased CD11c-CD206 adipose macrophage abundance, accompanied by elevated expression of alternative activation-associated markers. Together, these findings identify myeloid mDIC as an important regulator of macrophage mitochondrial function and adipose immune remodeling during obesity, suggesting a novel mechanism by which mitochondrial bioenergetics contribute to macrophage apoptotic-cell handling and metabolic homeostasis.

papers.title: Role of Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) in muscle fatigue: significance for muscle myopathies
papers.abstract: We report that Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) modulates skeletal muscle function. TLR2 ligands accelerated muscle fatigue development in isolated muscle fibers. Muscle fibers from TLR2 gene knock-out (TLR2-/-) mice were more fatigue resistant. This was not due to altered mitochondrial oxidative capacity or glycogen content. TLR2-/- muscle fibers had larger tetanic [Ca2+]i transients. Muscles from TLR2-/- mice had increased levels of Ca2+-binding proteins compared to WT muscles. Lastly, TLR2 was expressed in muscle fibers of control subjects and patients with idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM), whereas high mobility group box protein (HMGB) 1, an endogenous activator of TLR2, was only detected in the cytoplasm of muscles from IIM patients. In conclusion, TLR2 signaling regulates force production in skeletal muscle. TLR2 and its endogenous ligand, HMGB1 likely contribute to the muscle weakness in IIM and, possibly, other muscle disorders. Therapies targeted to the TLR2 signaling pathway may counteract pathological muscle weakness.

papers.title: Posterior Staphyloma-associated vitreous proteomic remodeling in high myopia
papers.abstract: Posterior staphyloma is a hallmark of pathologic myopia, but the cellular and molecular changes of the overlying retina remain poorly understood. We combined the histopathology of human eyes with posterior staphyloma with label-free proteomics of vitreous from non-myopic eyes (n = 4) and highly myopic eyes without (n = 3) or with posterior staphyloma (n = 7) and measured soluble vitreous iron in an independent series of 31 eyes. In the staphyloma, the retina collapsed at the transition zones into a vimentin- and GFAP-positive glial scar containing Iba1-positive microglia, with iron deposits, increased ferritin and disorganized scleral collagen. The vitreous proteome was not globally altered, but protein modules defined a priori to mirror these lesions revealed an activation of the classical complement pathway and an increased ferritin-to-transferrin ratio, both specific to staphylomatous eyes, whereas neuron- and photoreceptor-derived proteins were already decreased in highly myopic eyes without staphyloma. Soluble vitreous iron was lower in staphylomatous eyes than in non-myopic eyes and in highly myopic eyes without staphyloma, independently of total protein content. These findings suggest that complement activation and iron sequestration characterize the retinal degeneration associated with posterior staphyloma, and that the vitreous provides a window on these processes.

papers.title: The cost of stressing the royal family: parental glucocorticoid exposure has delayed adverse effects on chick physiology and survival in king penguins
papers.abstract: When exposed to stressful environmental conditions, adults of long-lived species may favour self-maintenance at the expense of reproductive investment. In breeding king penguins (Aptenodytes patagonicus), we previously showed that prolonged glucocorticoid hormone exposure during early breeding resulted in surprisingly little effect on parental self-maintenance. Here, we investigate whether the potential costs of this experimental stressor could be transferred to offspring through altered parental care, negatively affecting their growth, physiology and survival. We exposed parents to a ca. 1-month elevation in corticosterone and monitored parental investment and offspring performance over one year, from incubation to fledging. Corticosterone-treated parents exhibited reduced prolactin levels and spent less time at sea, highlighting alterations in both endocrine and behavioural processes supporting parental investment. Yet, parental care behaviour, hatching success and chick body mass/size were not significantly impacted. Major delayed costs of the parental treatment were however evident, as chicks from corticosterone-treated parents exhibited accelerated postnatal telomere shortening and faced nearly twice the mortality hazard of chicks from placebo-treated parents. By revealing the hidden reproductive costs of apparent parental resilience, our study challenges how we assess the consequences of environmental stressors in long-lived species, particularly when their effects only emerge long after exposure.

papers.title: Determination of mitochondrial matrix pH during ischemia-reperfusion injury in the isolated mouse heart using a genetically encoded fluorescent sensor
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial matrix pH (pHmtx) regulates cellular energetics, metabolite flux, and ion transport. Despite its importance in cellular energy metabolism and disease, pHmtx remains difficult to measure in the intact heart because pH-sensitive dyes are challenging to selectively target to the mitochondrial matrix. Changes in intracellular pH during cardiac ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) are significant and understanding pHmtx dynamics I/R would provide insight into mechanisms of injury. To overcome uncertainties associated with intracellular dye distribution, the pH-sensitive green fluorescent protein SypHer3 was stably expressed in the mitochondrial matrix of the adult mouse heart using adeno-associated virus (AAV). The isolated perfused heart was subjected to global no-flow ischemia, followed by reperfusion and SypHer3 fluorescence measured using an optical integrating sphere. Calibration of SypHer3 fluorescence fold-change against pH in isolated mitochondria enabled pHmtx quantification from SypHer3 fluorescence in the intact heart, based on an assigned starting pH of 7.47. We found that pHmtx decreased from 7.45 {+/-} 0.01 (n=5) during normoxia to 6.61 {+/-} 0.20 (n=5) after 20 minutes of ischemia, and reached 7.16 {+/-} 0.01 (n=5) within 1 minute of reperfusion. In paired experiments, we measured relative changes in mitochondrial Ca2+ (Ca2+m) in the isolated heart during I/R using the genetically encoded, mitochondrial-targeted Ca2+ sensor R-GECO1. Because R-GECO1 fluorescence is pH-sensitive, quantification of pHmtx is required to correct R-GECO1 fluorescence for pH-dependent effects. With correction for pH, R-GECO1 fluorescence increased 1.77 {+/-} 0.40-fold (n=7) within 20 minutes of ischemia and returned to baseline within the first minute of reperfusion, consistent with an increase in Ca2+m during ischemia that reversed upon reperfusion. In summary, we developed a fluorescence approach for measuring pHmtx, a key determinant of mitochondrial energetics and ion transport, in the isolated perfused mouse heart, providing time resolved quantitative estimates of pHmtx during I/R. Furthermore, this work expands the application of fluorescent sensors for interrogating mitochondrial physiology in the intact heart by providing a framework for accounting for pH-dependent effects on probe fluorescence.

papers.title: Distinct calcium, sodium, and water programs characterize mouse and human connecting tubule
papers.abstract: The kidney connecting tubule lies between the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct. Even though short, it plays a key role in regulating calcium, sodium, and potassium excretion and water balance in health and disease. In rodents and humans, transitions between distal segments are gradual, making the assignment of functional properties to cell types difficult. To address this, we enriched mouse kidney distal tubule cells prior to performing single nucleus RNA-sequencing. Connecting tubule cells separated into three clusters, one expressed genes that are relevant to calcium transport, while another expressed genes that are relevant to water transport. The third was intermediate between the other two. While genes for electrogenic sodium transport were expressed throughout the connecting tubule, Hsd11b2, the gene responsible for aldosterone-responsiveness, was expressed primarily by the distal cluster. Immunocytochemistry confirmed the separation of calcium and water transport pathways and spatial transcriptomics confirmed the linear organization of this segment. Human transcriptomic data showed similar gene separation. The results show that rodent and human connecting tubules separate calcium and water transport, thereby limiting tubule fluid calcium accumulation. They also restrict aldosterone action to segments that are responsive to arginine vasopressin to maintain sodium homeostasis during antidiuresis.

papers.title: Mitochondrial Dynamics Modulation via MyoAAV-Mediated OPA1 Overexpression or BNIP3 Knockdown in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC)-Induced Cachexia
papers.abstract: Disruption of mitochondrial dynamics and quality control precedes overt muscle wasting in cancer cachexia, but whether modulating it specifically in muscle in the presence of systemic wasting could preserve tissue mass and function remain elusive. We tested two independent, but complementary approaches in the orthotopic preclinical model of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (KPC); inducing inner-mitochondrial membrane fusion through OPA1 overexpression and suppressing mitophagy via BNIP3 knockdown. Male and female C57BL/6J mice received bilateral intramuscular tibialis anterior (TA) injections of myotropic adeno-associated virus (MyoAAV) encoding murine either OPA1 cDNA or a BNIP3-targeting short hairpin RNA two weeks prior to orthotopic implantation of KPC1245 pancreatic cancer cells. Raw body and tissue weights, in vivo dorsiflexor torque and fatigability, TA fiber size and type, protein fractional synthesis rate, oxidative histochemistry, and selected molecular markers were assessed at the humane endpoint. Neither intervention prevented systemic wasting, however, in males, OPA1 overexpression partially attenuated TA mass loss, relieved torque deficits, and restored the proportion of type IIB fibers. Females developed a milder cachectic phenotype; OPA1 overexpression increased TA mass and shifted fiber composition toward type IIA fibers without any changes in torque. In males, BNIP3 knockdown markedly improved torque, restored fatigue resistance, preserved type IIB fiber proportion, and lowered DRP1 protein. Functional benefits concurred by BNIP3 shRNA delivery were accompanied by lower mixed-protein synthesis in both sexes. These findings support mitochondrial quality control as a therapeutic target while indicating that effective treatment will require calibrated, rather than maximal, suppression of mitochondrial turnover.

papers.title: Macula densa-targeting gene delivery in vivo using AAV9
papers.abstract: Macula densa (MD) cells are key sensory and regulatory cells in the kidney; however, they have been difficult to study because of a lack of cell-specific, user-friendly in vivo research tools. Here we demonstrate the high affinity of wild-type Adeno-Associated Virus serotype 9 (AAV9) for MD cells and the feasibility of AAV9-mediated MD cell-specific genetic manipulations when administered to neonatal mice or after a temporary physiological challenge (low-salt diet) in the adult. A single intraperitoneal injection of low-dose AAV9-GFP given to neonatal mice on postnatal days P2-3 resulted in highly MD-specific and efficient transduction (~85% of all GFP+ cells were Nos1+ MD cells). Proof-of-concept studies used AAV9 to overexpress or knock down biologically relevant genes in MD cells and establish MD gain- and loss-of-function (Gof/Lof) mouse models for initial functional and structural phenotyping using intravital multiphoton microscopy at the single-nephron level and immunofluorescence-based histological analysis. RNAscope confirmed the MD-specific knockdown of Pregnancy-associated plasma protein A2 (Pappa2) expression by AAV9-Pappa2 shRNA treatment in MD-Pappa2Lof mice, and the MD-specific overexpression of Cell communication network 1 (Ccn1) by AAV9-Ccn1 mRNA treatment in MD-Ccn1Gof mice. The mouse phenotypes revealed alterations in classic MD/juxtaglomerular functions (renin control and tubuloglomerular feedback-mediated glomerular hemodynamics) as well as in newly emerging MD cell functions (tissue remodeling). MD-specific genetic manipulations in vivo via AAV9-mediated gene delivery may enable future studies of MD cell functions, including the MD program for endogenous kidney tissue remodeling and regeneration, and support the development of MD cell-targeting gene therapies for kidney diseases.

papers.title: Circadian rhythm in the atrioventricular node - in electrophysiology, contractility, metabolism, intracellular signalling and extracellular matrix
papers.abstract: The atrioventricular (AV) node shows a circadian rhythm-during sleep the PR interval is longer (because conduction velocity is decreased) and AV block is more common. We show the rhythm is similar in mouse and human, and using mice we have investigated the cause. There was still a rhythm in Kcnj5 knockout mice ruling out a major role of vagal tone (the vagus regulates the node via Kcnj5). Instead, we show the presence of a functioning circadian clock in the node (e.g. by detection of rhythmic clock transcripts). There was ~43-52% reduction in the rhythm of the PR interval on inhibition of the clock in a Bmal1 knockout mouse. There was a significant rhythm in >300 intracellular signalling molecules presumably driven by the clock and perhaps extrinsic signals. Downstream of the clock and signalling molecules, there was a rhythm in many transcripts and proteins (of 4,186 proteins, ~15% had a rhythm), responsible for example for contractile machinery, metabolism, extracellular matrix, and importantly ion channels. Ultimately, the PR interval is determined by ion channels, and there were rhythms in ion channels and ionic currents. A key determinant of conduction velocity is the upstroke velocity of the Ca2+-dependent nodal action potential and this was significantly reduced during sleep, this can be explained by reduced expression of Ca2+ channel subunits and a smaller L-type Ca2+ current at this time and this was confirmed by biophysically-detailed computer modelling. In conclusion, there is day-night molecular remodelling of the AV node and this is largely responsible for the circadian rhythm in the PR interval.

papers.title: Estradiol Signaling in Regulatory T Cells Coordinates the Remodeling of the Maternal Small Intestine during Pregnancy
papers.abstract: Pregnancy requires coordinated maternal adaptations to support fetal growth, yet signals that couple gestation to intestinal remodeling remain poorly defined. Here, we show that pregnancy induces a reversible regenerative program in the small intestine characterized by villus elongation, increased nutrient transporter expression, and enhanced absorptive capacity driven by intestinal stem cell (ISC) hyperproliferation. Using single-cell transcriptomic and genetic approaches, we identify intestinal regulatory T (Treg) cells as required regulators of this remodeling. Estradiol treatment of ovariectomized mice fully recapitulated the gestational intestinal remodeling phenotype, whereas Treg-specific deletion of estrogen receptor reduced villus expansion and impaired nutrient absorption. Mechanistically, elevated estradiol levels during pregnancy expand Treg cells and enhance IL-10 production, which directly promotes ISC proliferation and epithelial renewal. Cross-species analyses in mice and pigs support conservation of the intestinal phenotype, while integration of human GWAS data links Treg-associated IL-10 signaling to birth-weight-associated traits. Together, these findings demonstrate that pregnancy repurposes immune tolerance pathways to coordinate maternal intestinal remodeling with fetal nutritional demands.

papers.title: Insulin signaling in pericytes is a master regulator of endocrine and vascular niches in pancreatic islets
papers.abstract: Insulin plays a crucial role in lowering glycemia, but it is also a powerful anabolic hormone with potent effects on the vasculature. Most studies on insulin vascular actions have focused on endothelial cells. Much less is known about its effects on the mural cells of the microvasculature known as pericytes. This gap in knowledge is particularly relevant for the pancreatic islet microvasculature which is exposed to high insulin levels and relies on local pericytes to efficiently deliver its glucoregulatory hormones. To investigate how insulin affects islet pericyte function and the impact on glucose homeostasis, we generated mice that lack insulin receptors in pericytes (PerIRKO). Loss of insulin signaling in pericytes raised insulin levels, induced islet expansion and beta cell proliferation in the pancreas and in intraocular islet grafts from PerIRKO mice. These changes in beta cell numbers were accompanied by increased islet vascular density, although capillaries were dysfunctional ex vivo, compromising islet hormonal responses to an intravenous glucose challenge. Our study supports that insulin itself regulates islet endocrine and vascular niches through previously unrecognized actions on pericytes, revealing a novel mechanism that links the vasculature to endocrine homeostasis.

papers.title: A brief breathing challenge reveals a cardiac correlate of generalized anxiety beyond resting physiology and interoceptive measures
papers.abstract: Physiological markers measured at rest, such as heart rate variability, have proved relatively weak predictors of mental health symptoms. One potential reason is that resting measures are influenced by uncontrolled state factors, such as spontaneous breathing, whereas a standardized challenge holds these constant and may reveal regulatory differences not evident at rest. Here we asked whether respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) during slow paced breathing, a challenge that strongly increases RSA, carries information about symptoms beyond resting RSA and interoceptive measures. In 207 young adults (mean age 23.6 years, SD = 3.1), electrocardiogram (ECG) was recorded at rest and during slow (6 breaths/min) and fast (20 breaths/min) paced breathing. Lower RSA during slow breathing, relative to that predicted by resting RSA, was associated with more severe generalized anxiety symptoms ({beta} = -0.21, BF = 13), also when depressive symptoms were controlled, whereas resting RSA was not. The association was concentrated among participants with at least moderate anxiety symptoms, whose resting RSA was typical but whose rest-adjusted slow-breathing RSA was 0.62 SD lower, and who in exploratory analyses also showed weaker phase coupling between heart period and respiration. Interoceptive accuracy, measured with heartbeat counting or heart rate discrimination, was unrelated to symptoms, self-report and slow-breathing RSA, and interoceptive questionnaires tracked distress shared across anxiety and depressive symptoms rather than generalized anxiety symptoms. At the group level, slow-breathing RSA thus carries information about generalized anxiety symptoms beyond resting RSA and self-reported interoception. Brief paced-breathing challenges may therefore increase the sensitivity of autonomic markers in anxiety research and merit testing in clinical samples.

papers.title: Aging exacerbates muscle loss induced by semaglutide treatment in female mice
papers.abstract: Background Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), including semaglutide, have transformed the pharmacological treatment of obesity. While highly efficacious in promoting weight loss, these drugs also induce substantial reductions in lean mass, raising concerns for skeletal muscle loss, particularly in older individuals vulnerable to sarcopenia. Nevertheless, there are currently no published human studies that investigated the effects of GLP-1RAs on skeletal muscle mass using gold standard methods. Meanwhile, studies in young mice demonstrate that skeletal muscle loss induced by GLP-1RAs might not be a major concern. The purpose of the current study was to investigate the effects of semaglutide on skeletal muscle mass and strength in aged mice. Methods Eighteen-month-old male and female C57BL/6J mice were fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 12 weeks to induce obesity. At 21 months of age, mice received daily subcutaneous injections of vehicle or semaglutide (3 or 30 nmol/kg) for 3 weeks. Body composition was assessed weekly by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. After 3 wks, mice were terminated to assess masses of individual organs including skeletal muscle. Skeletal muscle force-generating capacity was assessed by ex vivo electrical stimulation-induced contraction. Myofiber cross-sectional area and fiber-type composition were also assessed. Results Semaglutide induced dose-dependent weight loss in both sexes, with reductions of 11.3% and 20.2% in males and 21.1% and 26.1% in females receiving 3 or 30 nmol/kg dose, respectively. There was a substantial sex-difference in the loss of lean mass, with relatively minor reductions in males (2.3% and 6.6%) and greater loss in females (8.6% and 8.3%). Skeletal muscle mass was largely preserved in males but females exhibited greater muscle mass loss, including 14.2% reduction in quadriceps mass at 30 nmol/kg of semaglutide treatment. In contrast, skeletal muscle force-generating capacity was not compromised in semaglutide-treated females, while males exhibited 19.2% reduction in force generating capacity of the extensor digitorum longus (EDL) muscles at the 30 nmol/kg dose. Conclusion Unlike young mice, semaglutide treatment may induce meaningful loss in skeletal muscle mass in aged female mice and muscle strength in aged male mice. These findings highlight the importance of considering age as a potential factor that may negatively influence muscle mass and function in humans treated with GLP-1RAs. Clinical studies examining the influence of pharmacological weight loss on skeletal muscle mass and strength should consider both age and sex as a potentially important determinant of these outcomes.

papers.title: Perinatal high-fat diet induces systemic inflammation via altered tight junction complex organization during development and decreases expression of intestinal satiety peptides in male offspring.
papers.abstract: Objective Epidemiological evidence suggests that maternal obesity increases risk for offspring obesity and comorbidities, pointing to the significance of critical periods of development. Adverse metabolic effects of high fat (HF) diet consumption on the gut microbiome and inflammation have been well documented in obesity models. Emerging evidence demonstrates that the gut microbiome may play a role in transgenerational obesity, however, underlying mechanisms still need to be elucidated to identify intervention targets. Methods A rat model was used to demonstrate whether maternal HF diet during gestation and lactation results in gut-brain axis deficits in rat offspring. Gene expression of small intestinal satiety hormones and C-fiber innervation in the nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS) were measured in adult offspring. At weaning, circulating inflammatory mediators and colonic microbial metabolites were measured in offspring. Results In adulthood, HF males had reduced vagal innervation in the NTS and reduced small intestinal expression of CCK, GLP-1, and PYY. At weaning, HF offspring had elevated levels of CRP and IL-1{beta} and depleted levels of microbially produced colonic short chain fatty acids (SCFAs), which are critical for maintaining intestinal barrier function. HF males had reduced colocalization between tight junction proteins, Claudin-1 and ZO-1 at weaning, while HF females did not. Conclusion Disorganization of tight junction complexes in HF male offspring during development may play a role in the gut-brain axis deficits seen in HF males in adulthood. Together, these data demonstrate that inflammation-induced by HF diet can negatively impact gut-brain axis development and function.

papers.title: High +Gz Exposure Alters Urinary Extracellular Vesicle miRNAs in Humans
papers.abstract: High +Gz exposure elicits complex cardiovascular, autonomic, and endocrine responses, but the associated molecular responses in humans remain poorly understood. We investigated whether microRNAs (miRNAs) encapsulated in urinary extracellular vesicles (uEVs) are altered following acute high +Gz exposure. Twenty-one healthy young men undergoing human centrifuge training provided urine samples before, immediately after, and on the morning after exposure. Candidate uEV-encapsulated miRNAs were identified by RNA sequencing and Gene Ontology analysis, and 16 miRNAs related to ischemia, hypoxia, blood pressure regulation, and mechanical stress were quantified by quantitative PCR. Salivary cortisol, urinary catecholamines, and heart rate were also assessed. Six uEV-encapsulated miRNAs increased significantly after high +Gz exposure. miR-20b-5p, miR-125b-5p, and miR-130a-3p increased immediately after exposure and returned to baseline by the following morning, whereas miR-335-5p, miR-17-5p, and miR-92a-3p remained elevated. Urinary adrenaline, noradrenaline, and dopamine increased immediately after exposure; adrenaline returned to baseline by the following morning, whereas noradrenaline and dopamine remained elevated. Salivary cortisol and heart rate also increased. These findings demonstrate distinct transient and sustained temporal responses of uEV-encapsulated miRNAs to high +Gz in humans, paralleling different catecholamine response patterns. Although their tissue origins and functional roles remain unresolved, these findings provide new molecular-level insights into the human physiological response to high +Gz.

papers.title: Light-induced melatonin suppression in school-aged children before and during camping: associations with circadian phase and daytime light exposure
papers.abstract: Prior light exposure can influence the magnitude of melatonin suppression in response to evening light, even within the same individual. We examined whether light-induced melatonin suppression in school-aged children differed before and during a camp with approximately two weeks of exposure to a natural light-dark cycle. We also explored interindividual variation in melatonin suppression and its associations with circadian phase, habitual sleep timing, and daytime light exposure. Twenty-one healthy children aged 9--14 years underwent evening light experiments at the start of camp (Pre-camp session) and approximately two weeks later (Camp session). Melatonin suppression was calculated by comparing the area under the melatonin concentration curve between the evening light condition (200 {+/-} 30 lx, 5000 K) and the dim light condition (< 30 lx, incandescent lamps), with integration starting at dim light melatonin onset (DLMO). We assessed sleep habits from 14-day sleep diaries before camping and measured wrist-level illuminance during camping. We examined associations using Spearman correlations and compared Pre-camp and Camp melatonin suppression using a paired t-test. Melatonin suppression did not differ significantly between Pre-camp and Camp sessions (p = 0.21). Greater suppression in the Pre-camp session was associated with later DLMO (rho = 0.49, p = 0.028), but not with habitual sleep variables. In the Camp session, higher same-day geometric mean illuminance was associated with lower suppression (n = 15; rho = -0.58, p = 0.024), whereas 7-day light-exposure metrics were not. Mean melatonin suppression did not significantly change across the camping period. Meanwhile, children showed large interindividual variation in melatonin suppression, and circadian phase and recent daytime light exposure are candidate correlates of this variation in the responsiveness to the evening light.

papers.title: Sex differences in myocardial ketone oxidation capacity in cardiometabolic disease with coincident ischemic heart disease
papers.abstract: Background: Myocardial infarction (MI) in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is associated with worse outcomes than MI in individuals without HFpEF. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying this increased vulnerability remain poorly understood. We investigated sex differences in cardiac ketone body (KB) metabolism in patients with diabetes-associated ischemic heart disease, and in a mouse model of HFpEF complicated by MI (HFpEF-MI). Methods: Cardiac BDH1 and OXCT1 expression was assessed in male and female patients with diabetes, with or without ischemic heart disease. Male and female mice received a high-fat diet and L-NAME for 10 weeks to induce HFpEF, followed by coronary artery ligation to induce MI. Glucose tolerance, cardiac function, survival, cardiac KB oxidative capacity, and circulating KB levels were evaluated. Results: Cardiac BDH1 and OXCT1 abundance was significantly reduced in male patients with diabetes-associated ischemic heart disease but preserved in female patients. In mice, 10 weeks of high-fat diet and L-NAME administration increased fasting blood glucose and impaired glucose tolerance. MI reduced systolic function in control and HFpEF mice of both sexes. Male HFpEF-MI mice exhibited higher mortality than female HFpEF-MI mice. Consistent with our human results, male HFpEF-MI mice showed reduced cardiac ketolytic enzyme expression alongside elevated circulating KB levels, whereas female mice maintained cardiac KB oxidative capacity. Conclusion: Reduced cardiac ketolytic enzyme expression and impaired KB oxidative capacity are associated with greater mortality in male HFpEF-MI mice, whereas female mice exhibit preserved KB oxidative capacity and improved survival. Similar sex differences in ketolytic enzyme expression were observed in patients with diabetes-associated ischemic heart disease. These findings identify cardiac ketone metabolism as a potential therapeutic target warranting further investigation in HFpEF complicated by MI.

papers.title: Lipidomic analysis of postprandial mesenteric lymph from wild type and Dennd5b knockout mice.
papers.abstract: Chylomicrons are intestine-derived lipoproteins that transport dietary lipids from the intestine to the systemic circulation. Although the composition of chylomicrons may influence their peripheral metabolism and biological functions, the lipid composition of newly secreted chylomicrons remains incompletely characterized. In this study, we combined a conscious mesenteric lymph fistula model with mass spectrometry-based lipidomics to characterize changes in the intestinal lymph lipidome following duodenal lipid administration in wild type and Dennd5b-deficient mice, a model of impaired intestinal chylomicron secretion. In wild type mice, lipid administration significantly increased lymphatic triglyceride output and altered the abundance of multiple lipid species, including glycerolipids, glycerophospholipids, and sphingolipids. Notably, ceramides and hexosylceramides exhibited disproportionate increases relative to their abundance in the administered lipid. In contrast, Dennd5b-deficient mice exhibited a near-complete blunting of the postprandial lymphatic lipidomic response, with markedly attenuated export across multiple lipid classes. Genotype-dependent differences were also evident in baseline lymph, indicating that Dennd5b influences lymphatic lipid composition under both basal and postprandial conditions. Together, these findings demonstrate that the physiological impact of Dennd5b deficiency on intestinal lipid trafficking extends well beyond triglycerides, underscoring an essential role for Dennd5b-dependent chylomicron secretion in the coordinated lymphatic export of dietary and endogenous lipids.

papers.title: Dietary Human HSP90 Promotes Longevity and Healthspan in Caenorhabditis elegans via a Multi-Branched Stress Signaling Pathway
papers.abstract: The loss of proteostasis is one of the primary drivers of aging. Despite the important role of the molecular chaperone HSP90 in maintaining proteostasis, its systemic role in aging appears contradictory because its inhibitors can effectively extend lifespan across diverse species. This study showed that dietary HSP90 supplementation via Escherichia coli significantly extended lifespan and healthspan of Caenorhabditis elegans without fertility trade-offs. Exogenous HSP90 likely acts as an extracellular signaling ligand that engages downstream kinase networks to drive the activation of three major longevity-associated transcription factors: DAF-16, SKN-1, and HSF-1. In addition, we demonstrated the additive effect of combining dietary HSP90 supplementation with the senolytic HSP90 inhibitor tanespimycin, indicating that extracellular proteostatic signaling and the intracellular inhibition of HSP90 can work together to enhance longevity. Finally, we engineered an antibiotic-free E. coli Nissle 1917 probiotic that constitutively expresses HSP90, which successfully extended the lifespan of C. elegans.

papers.title: The canine hair metabolome encodes age and coat exposure in over 700 dogs
papers.abstract: Hair can be collected noninvasively and stored for years, making it a practical sample for studying physiology and environmental exposure. Yet the chemical information it carries in dogs remains largely unexplored. We profiled 782 banked hair samples from 700 Golden Retrievers by untargeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, detecting 4,533 compound groups and revealing an unexpectedly rich chemical profile. Prominent signals reflected skin-surface and hair chemistry, including amino acids, peptides and urocanic acid, alongside surfactants, plasticizers and pesticides detectable despite washing. A signal annotated as imidacloprid distinguished dogs receiving topical products containing this insecticide from dogs receiving no flea or tick preventive (AUC 0.865). Hair chemistry also varied with age, most strongly between puppyhood and early adulthood. Oxidized lipids generally declined, whereas amino acids and peptides remained largely stable. A multivariate model estimated age with moderate accuracy (cross-validated r = 0.66) and assigned a higher age to the later sample in 64 of 75 repeatedly sampled dogs. Because age and collection date were strongly correlated, their effects could not be fully separated, although date-restricted analyses supported an age-related contribution. Together, these findings establish banked dog hair as a promising resource for studying chemical exposure and life-stage-associated changes in chemistry.

papers.title: Cell wall composition drives off-target sensitivity to indaziflam
papers.abstract: Indaziflam is a potent alkylazine herbicide classified as a cellulose biosynthesis inhibitor (CBI) with broad-spectrum pre-emergence activity and long soil persistence. While its efficacy in commercial weed control is established, its off-target ecological footprint across taxa with non-cellulose cell wall compositions remains poorly defined. We evaluated the potential off-target biological impacts of indaziflam across organisms representing distinct cell wall architectures, including the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (chitin/glucan), the unicellular alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii (glycoprotein), and the early-diverging bryophyte Marchantia polymorpha (cellulose/hemicellulose/pectin). Indaziflam did not inhibit the growth of non-target organisms lacking plant-type cellulose cell walls. In S. cerevisiae, treatment unexpectedly accelerated growth rates to reach ED50 (12.95 h at 3200 pM vs. 16.23 h in control). Similarly, C. reinhardtii showed no growth suppression across concentration ranges up to 100 nM. Conversely, the non-vascular land plant M. polymorpha exhibited marked, dose-dependent sensitivity. In vitro, thallus surface area was significantly suppressed at concentrations above 1600 pM (p<0.05). In greenhouse trials, pre-emergence application of indaziflam at recommended (1X) and elevated (2X, 3X) field rates provided up to 100% control of liverwort establishment and biomass accumulation over an 8-week evaluation period. Off-target activity of indaziflam is strictly confined to land plants (Embryophytes) possessing conserved cellulose-containing cell walls, with no adverse growth effects observed in organisms featuring chitin- or glycoprotein-based wall structures. These findings clarify the selective environmental toxicity profile of indaziflam, demonstrating that its biological activity aligns closely with its CBI classification without causing widespread toxicity across non-plant soil organisms.

papers.title: 28S-rsRNA facilitates PASMC proliferation through PKM2 β-hydroxybutyrylation
papers.abstract: Ribosomal RNA-derived small RNAs (rsRNAs) are nucleic acid fragments originating from rRNA, the functions and roles of which in diseases remain incompletely understood. We identified 28S rsRNA-CTC_L20, an rsRNA whose expression is upregulated in hypoxic pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells (PASMCs) and in lung tissues of pulmonary hypertension (PH) models. In hypoxic cells, 28S rsRNA-CTC_L20 promotes PASMC proliferation, and its knockdown mitigates SuHx-induced pulmonary hypertension and vascular remodeling. Mechanistically, 28S rsRNA-CTC_L20 modulates {beta}-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) production by maintaining the stability of ketogenic enzyme mRNAs through its "CTGNNGG" motif. Elevated levels of BHB enhance the {beta}-hydroxybutyrylation modification at K166 of pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2), increasing its activity and driving glycolysis to sustain proliferation. These results link ketone body metabolism to glycolysis in hypoxic cells and define an rsRNA-BHB-PKM2 {beta}-hydroxybutyrylation axis in PH. They also point to 28S rsRNA-CTC_L20 as a potential target for treating vascular remodeling.

papers.title: Body weight modifies the efficacy of lifespan-extending interventions in ad libitum-fed mice
papers.abstract: Geroprotective interventions are often assessed by extension of lifespan in ad libitum-fed mice. Increased lifespan could therefore reflect rescue of adverse phenotypes of unhealthy controls. We analysed body weight and survival for 33,780 mice in the Interventions Testing Program (ITP) to test whether treatment effects varied with body weight. In males, each added standard deviation of attained adult weight made treatment 6% more favourable (HR 0.94), more apparent for interventions that lowered body weight (HR 0.90). Median lifespan increase rose from 6.2% in mice in the lightest quartile to 20.2% in the heaviest pre-dosing weight quartile among those experiments, mainly because control survival declined more steeply with weight than that of the intervention group. The effect of body weight was consistent across 13 of 14 compounds and reflected weight attained during adulthood rather than in early life. Weight-dependence of intervention effects was weak in ITP females, possibly because median survival of controls exceeded that of every sampled non-ITP female control group. Amelioration of weight-associated risk is therefore implicated as a major contributor to lifespan increases relative to heavy, short-lived controls. The geroprotective effects of these interventions may thus be less apparent in metabolically healthier mice or humans.

papers.title: Single-nucleus analysis reveals renal STAT1/CEBPB signaling as a modifiable relay of proinflammatory FGF23 effects in diabetic kidney disease
papers.abstract: Background Circulating fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) rises dramatically in chronic kidney disease, particularly in diabetic kidney disease (DKD). At high concentrations, and with declining Klotho, FGF23 has been linked to renal inflammation. The cell types and transcriptional programs mediating these off-target actions remain undefined. We asked whether the diseased kidney responds to FGF23 differently from the healthy kidney, and whether any disease-specific response could be targeted. Methods Male and female DBA/2J mice received streptozotocin or vehicle to induce DKD. On day 56, mice received a single dose intravenous injection of FGF23 (0.3 g) or vehicle, with tissue collected 1 h later for single-nucleus RNA sequencing, differential expression and regulon (inferred transcription factor activity) analysis. Candidate pathways were tested in precision-cut kidney slices using the CEBPB inhibitor ST-101. Results Streptozotocin-treated male mice developed early DKD with a 6-fold increase in urinary albumin/creatinine ratio and 50% higher blood urea nitrogen with preserved glomerular filtration rate. All major renal cell types were annotated. Canonical FGF23 signaling was intact in disease, with segment-specific target induction conserved in both conditions (e.g. Cyp24a1 in PT-S1 and DCT1). Superimposed on this were disease-restricted responses, including Wsb1 in DCT1 and Pdk4 in PT-S2, PST, DCT1 and DCT2. Regulon analysis revealed DKD-specific induction of CEBPB regulon activity by FGF23 across all analyzed tubular segments, and of STAT1 in several segments. Pre-treatment with a CEBPB inhibitor suppressed CEBPB activity, downstream NF-KB and pro-inflammatory gene sets, and immune-like cell abundance in diseased slices. Conclusion In the diabetic kidney, FGF23 engages a STAT1-CEBPB-NF-{kappa}B axis absent from healthy kidney and extending beyond its canonical Klotho-dependent target segments, identifying CEBPB as a potential treatment target for FGF23's pathological inflammatory actions.

papers.title: Selective activation of estrogen receptors modulates electrical activity and insulin secretion in human EndoC-βH1 cells
papers.abstract: Estrogen receptors (ERs), ER and ER{beta} have important roles in the physiology of the endocrine pancreas in animal models, but the effects of ER activation on insulin-secreting human cells are still poorly understood. Here, we investigated the role of ER and ER{beta} as modulators of electrical activity and insulin secretion in the insulin-secreting human cell line EndoC-{beta}H1. Immunocytochemical analysis revealed a widespread cellular distribution of ER, while ER{beta} was predominantly localized outside the nucleus. We observed that both estradiol (E2) and the ER{beta} agonist diarylpropionitrile (DPN) led to a decrease in insulin secretion in the absence of stimulatory glucose concentrations, without affecting insulin content. Patch-clamp experiments revealed that a 48-hour treatment with either the ER agonist PPT or DPN resulted in depolarization of the resting membrane potential, increased action potential firing frequency, and altered the action potential waveform in EndoC-{beta}H1 cells. PPT increased voltage-dependent Ca2+ channel currents, while DPN reduced K+ and Na+ currents. These results suggest that activation of ER and ER{beta} modulates beta-cell electrical activity through distinct pathways involving ion channels. The effects of E2, PPT, and DPN were not caused by altered expression levels of ion channel genes after 48 hours of treatment. This suggests that these receptors act extranuclearly without affecting gene expression. Together, our findings demonstrate that selective activation of ER and ER{beta} modulates beta-cell excitability through distinct electrophysiological mechanisms and that E2 and DPN reduce basal insulin secretion in human EndoC-{beta}H1 cells. These results support ER and ER{beta} as potential targets for modulating human pancreatic beta-cell function.

papers.title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
papers.abstract: Cardiac autonomic activity is observed only through beat-to-beat (RR) intervals, and separating it into parasympathetic-like and sympathetic-like components is an inverse problem that RR alone is not expected to solve uniquely. We introduce SPARK (Stochastic Phase-domain Autonomic Reconstruction Kinetics), a state-space model in which two independent, mean-reverting latent drives modulate heart rate through an integrate-and-fire pacemaker. The model is combined with exact continuous-time Kalman filtering and with an explicit physiological identification structure: time-scale priors, a kinetic ordering and a spectral partition of heart rate variability. SPARK offers a model-conditional description of autonomic trajectories that complements conventional heart rate variability; its latent states are reconstructions, not measurements of neural activity. Across recordings, fitting each recording from many different starting points gave a median of 23.5 distinct solutions without physiological information versus 1.0 with it, and one process absorbed essentially all the variability in 75% versus 4% of the fits; the fit diagnostics showed residual structure in most recordings. Reconstructions were then examined: in 10 tilt-table recordings, the vagal-like state decreased and the sympathetic-like state increased in 10 of 10; exploratory comparisons between 20 young and 20 older adults showed differences in reconstructed variability and faster-component kinetics, although several latent summaries were mathematically redundant; and in 263 exercise recordings, median recovery times, which are closely tied to the fitted time constants, were 42 s (vagal-like) and 341 s (sympathetic-like). How a stressor-induced change is split between the two drives remained sensitive to the spectral anchor.

papers.title: Skeletal muscle aging drives sex- and compartment-specific protein insolubility that is modifiable by proteostasis-directed treatments
papers.abstract: Protein aggregation and altered protein solubility indicate proteostatic decline, yet their roles in skeletal muscle aging remain poorly understood. We combined light and electron microscopy, quantitative proteomics, and stable-isotope labeling of skeletal muscle to investigate age-associated changes in protein insolubility, and their responses to exercise and rapamycin. Aged muscle accumulated distinct aggresome and amyloid-positive aggregates despite unchanged bulk insoluble protein content. Instead, aging altered the abundance and soluble-insoluble shifts of lower-abundance proteins across cellular components, particularly mitochondrial, nuclear and extracellular matrix proteins, with greater changes in females. These changes were not broadly explained by intrinsic protein aggregation propensity. Exercise and rapamycin partially reversed age-associated changes in abundance and partitioning without increasing protein synthesis. Together, these findings highlight sex- and cellular component-dependent changes in protein insolubility as important, modifiable aspects of skeletal muscle proteostasis, and indicate that proteostatic maintenance may be a more important target than anabolism for muscle aging.
